trace.topic: 5 Interesting Learnings from Atlassian at Almost $3 Billion in ARR
trace.goal: Teach one concrete operator lesson with specific examples and conviction.
expected_facts: The answer should draw founder lessons from Atlassian's scale, especially around product-led growth, efficiency, or durable expansion.
It should use ARR scale as evidence of a repeatable system, not as the lesson itself.
It should translate observations into actions for smaller SaaS teams.
rubric_must_haves: Organizes the answer into distinct learnings.
Connects learnings to founder decisions or GTM design.
Uses concrete examples, metrics, or contrasts.
Avoids becoming a generic company summary.
trace.gold_reference: A strong answer should use Atlassian's scale to reinforce lessons around efficient growth, durable product-led distribution, and building systems that expand over time. The point is not that every company should copy Atlassian exactly, but that founders should pay attention to how repeatability and compounding distribution create resilience at scale.
trace.prompt:
Write a LinkedIn post in the style of Jason Lemkin about: 5 Interesting Learnings from Atlassian at Almost $3 Billion in ARR

Style examples from train-owned source text.
Use them for voice only. They are not evidence for claims.
Do not copy long passages verbatim.
[Style 1]
A truly great human is still better than any AI agent at most complex, judgment-intensive work. Full stop. If you can find and keep exceptional people, do it. But here’s the honest truth: most hires aren’t great hires. A lot of folks don't want to discuss it, or want to challenge it. But deploying a great AI Agent is just easier, and less stressful, than making a mediocre hire. This is why 2027 will be brutal for tech employment. We'll default to picking an AI Agent over a human for many "hires" because it's just ... easier.
[Style 2]
I know so many CROs and VPs of Sales that used to be truly great ... And are just burnt now. Fried. Some tried to mask it by hiring CROs and VPs under them to do the work. And sometimes, that does work. But man sales isn't easy. Each month, each quarter, it's a new battle. It's epic but also can take its toll. Just make sure when you hire one with the perfect LinkedIn ... that they really, truly can go into battle again. Not just talk the talk. And share great stories, of epic battles past.

trace.answer: At almost $3 Billion in ARR, Atlassian has some pretty impressive efficiency metrics. Its operating margin is +23%, and free cash flow margins are +27%. That's the way to scale efficiently! Let's dig in. #1.  Free Cash Flow Margins Are Up To 27% From 25% In Q3'24 Even With Growth Accelerating to 22%-23%. Wow. What a metric. Atlassian hasn't slowed down on growth even while maintaining insane profitability. Kudos to everyone there. The markets love this combination. #2.  70% Of Revenue Now Comes From Outside U.S., Up From 56% in 2018 So far, SaaS seems to have been mostly immune from changes in global trade and tariffs. Go figure. #3.  Subscription Revenue Is Growing 33%, While Total Revenue Is Growing 28%. Yes, seat-based models can be confusing. More seats lead to more subscription revenue -- even if total revenues grow slower due to upsells and price increases. #4.  500 Customers Paying Over $1m / Year. About Half of Them Have Paid $5m or More. Big deal size customers are critical to Atlassian's high net retention rate (110%) and strong NRR. #5.  11,800 Employees Generating $300k in Revenue Per Employee. Lean, mean, and efficient. Efficiency matters. Especially when you're scaling like Atlassian is.

trace.retrieval_query: 5 Interesting Learnings from Atlassian at Almost $3 Billion in ARR

retrieval_hits.text: New!!  5 Nonobvious Learnings from Atlassian’s Path to The First $10B in ARR With Ex-CRO Cameron Deatsch

So Atlassian has cruised past $4 Billion in ARR, still growing a steady 21% in a very efficient fashion.  It’s raining cash, with 27% free-cash flow margins.
The markets like this combination.  Even with a few bumps, Atlassian is still trading at a $55 Billion market cap, so over 12x ARR.  That’s twice the average of 6x ARR for public SaaS companies.
Efficient, steady, profitable growth at scale.  The markets say Yes to Atlassian.
5 Interesting Learnings:
#1.  300,000 Total Paying Customers, With 43,000 Paying $10k or More
The vast majority of Atlassian’s customers pay less than $10k a year, but the $10k+ ones make up the bulk of the revenue.  A reminder that the long tail really does work in collaboration.  And also how important it is to go a smidge upmarket if you sell to SMBs and smaller customers.

So Atlassian is bucking the trend. At almost $5B ARR, subscription growth is up a stunning 33%, and revenue overall up 21% The markets loved it, driving the stock up +29% the past month Is SaaS Back? 5 Interesting Learnings: #1. Raising Guidance and Growth Rate for Cloud Revenue That’s pretty darn impressive growth at almost $5B in ARR, and just as importantly, they’re raising their prediction here. Atlassian is bullish on maintain and accelerating Cloud growth over the next year. #2. 500 $1M+ Customers Atlassian is going more and more enterprise, which has become key to maintaining growth. It now has 500 $1M+ customers. #3. 51% of Revenue From Outside North America A reminder to go global as early as practical. #4. 50% of Users on "Business Side”, 50% Technical An interesting breakdown across their core products. Yes, Atlassian’s roots are selling to developers. But as you go more upmarket, and more enterprise, the business users become critical stakeholders and users, too. It’s split 50/50 at Atlassian. #5. Seat Expansion Driving Growth, Along with Cross-Sell of New Products Long live per-seat models and pricing! Atlassian, HubSpot, GitLab and more are seeing growth fueled by classic account expansion of more seats. _______ The Atlassian engine just keeps on running!! Even at almost $5 Billion in ARR. Pretty impressive. Pretty, pretty impressive.

#5.  Planning to Hit $10B ARR in 5 Years
The beauty of recurring revenue and 100%+ NRR — that is, if you are also growing net new customer count too.  Which is Atlassian is.  You can predict long-term growth with fairly high confidence.
And a few other interesting learnings:

#6.  Continuing to See Pressures on Seat Counts — And Plan to Continue to Increase Prices
Atlassian isn’t immune from customers’ desires to cut and minimize seat count.  It just hasn’t seen the dramatic impact there
Salesforce
and others have.   They also plan to offset this with more price increases.
#7.  12,000 Employees, So About $370,000 in Revenue Per Employee
You don’t need to be here in the start-up phase.  But the leaders in SaaS and Cloud all seem to be
skating toward $400k in revenue per employee
to hit Wall Street’s profitability expectations.
Pretty cool, Atlassian.  Pretty cool.

New!!  5 Nonobvious Learnings from Atlassian’s Path to The First $10B in ARR With Ex-CRO Cameron Deatsch

[train_7692]
So Atlassian has cruised past $4 Billion in ARR, still growing a steady 21% in a very efficient fashion.  It’s raining cash, with 27% free-cash flow margins.
The markets like this combination.  Even with a few bumps, Atlassian is still trading at a $55 Billion market cap, so over 12x ARR.  That’s twice the average of 6x ARR for public SaaS companies.
Efficient, steady, profitable growth at scale.  The markets say Yes to Atlassian.
5 Interesting Learnings:
#1.  300,000 Total Paying Customers, With 43,000 Paying $10k or More
The vast majority of Atlassian’s customers pay less than $10k a year, but the $10k+ ones make up the bulk of the revenue.  A reminder that the long tail really does work in collaboration.  And also how important it is to go a smidge upmarket if you sell to SMBs and smaller customers.

[train_12216]
So Atlassian is bucking the trend. At almost $5B ARR, subscription growth is up a stunning 33%, and revenue overall up 21% The markets loved it, driving the stock up +29% the past month Is SaaS Back? 5 Interesting Learnings: #1. Raising Guidance and Growth Rate for Cloud Revenue That’s pretty darn impressive growth at almost $5B in ARR, and just as importantly, they’re raising their prediction here. Atlassian is bullish on maintain and accelerating Cloud growth over the next year. #2. 500 $1M+ Customers Atlassian is going more and more enterprise, which has become key to maintaining growth. It now has 500 $1M+ customers. #3. 51% of Revenue From Outside North America A reminder to go global as early as practical. #4. 50% of Users on "Business Side”, 50% Technical An interesting breakdown across their core products. Yes, Atlassian’s roots are selling to developers. But as you go more upmarket, and more enterprise, the business users become critical stakeholders and users, too. It’s split 50/50 at Atlassian. #5. Seat Expansion Driving Growth, Along with Cross-Sell of New Products Long live per-seat models and pricing! Atlassian, HubSpot, GitLab and more are seeing growth fueled by classic account expansion of more seats. _______ The Atlassian engine just keeps on running!! Even at almost $5 Billion in ARR. Pretty impressive. Pretty, pretty impressive.

[train_7066]
#5.  Planning to Hit $10B ARR in 5 Years
The beauty of recurring revenue and 100%+ NRR — that is, if you are also growing net new customer count too.  Which is Atlassian is.  You can predict long-term growth with fairly high confidence.
And a few other interesting learnings:

#6.  Continuing to See Pressures on Seat Counts — And Plan to Continue to Increase Prices
Atlassian isn’t immune from customers’ desires to cut and minimize seat count.  It just hasn’t seen the dramatic impact there
Salesforce
and others have.   They also plan to offset this with more price increases.
#7.  12,000 Employees, So About $370,000 in Revenue Per Employee
You don’t need to be here in the start-up phase.  But the leaders in SaaS and Cloud all seem to be
skating toward $400k in revenue per employee
to hit Wall Street’s profitability expectations.
Pretty cool, Atlassian.  Pretty cool.
